newsitem.title: USA: Gingrich ethics problems mount as lawyer quits.
newsitem.headline: Gingrich ethics problems mount as lawyer quits.

text.p: House Speaker Newt Gingrich's ethics problems mounted Thursday after he was dropped by the lawyer who has been representing him before the House ethics committee.

The departure of attorney Jan Baran, apparently in a dispute over accuracy of information provided to investigators, prompted a demand by Gingrich's chief Democratic opponent that he "come clean" before the House is asked to re-elect him as speaker Jan. 7.
"The speaker should lay all the facts out and level with his colleagues," Democratic Whip David Bonior told reporters.
"The vote (for speaker) ought to be made with all the facts and knowledge available to all of us."
The lawyer, Jan Baran has said he dropped Gingrich as a client Saturday, following a series of closed-door meetings of an ethics subcommittee that has been looking into allegations against Gingrich.
Baran also has said his firm did not submit any information to the ethics committee without Gingrich's prior review and approval, and he believed this was also the committee's view.

Since September the four-member ethics subcommittee has been investigating whether Gingrich provided "accurate, reliable and complete information" about his college course or a tax-free foundation "in the course of communicating with the committee, either directly or through counsel."
It added this issue to its investigation into whether Gingrich broke federal tax laws barring use of tax-exempt charities for partisan political purposes in the college course he taught.
Gingrich has vigorously denied any wrongdoing.
Baran has been replaced by Atlanta attorney Randolph Evans, a legal malpractice specialist from Atlanta who frequently lectures on ethics and malpractice.
The sudden switch in Gingrich's attorneys could prolong the investigation. But Bonior called on Gingrich to make a public statement before the speakership vote Jan. 7.

"It's always been a sign of trouble when a client fires his attorney. But when an attorney fires a client, that's about as bad as it gets," Bonior said. "It's time for Newt Gingrich to come clean with the American people."

Bonior noted that a close ally of Gingrich, Representative John Linder, a Georgia Republican, had told a reporter that Gingrich had in fact signed an erroneous statement to the subcommittee but that the error had been made by Baran.
Bonior said this meant Gingrich "is trying to pin all of this on his attorney."
The investigating subcommittee wound up a series of meetings last Friday before members left town amid speculation that it had completed its work and notified Gingrich of its findings.

Neither the panel nor Gingrich's office would discuss the investigation, although the Wall Street Journal has reported that the panel's special counsel, James Cole, has recommended that Gingrich be charged with violations.

Under the ethics committee's rules, if the subcommittee finds "reason to believe" there had been wrongdoing, it would send a statement of alleged violation to Gingrich, who would have 30 days to respond.
Such a statement is something like an indictment and would be followed by a "trial" conducted by the other six members of the full ethics committee.
If the offence is proved, the full committee could then recommend punishment ranging from a letter of reproval to expulsion from the House.

The election of the speaker takes place at the start of each two-year congressional session. The Republicans, who have a 20-seat majority in the House, have already renominated Gingrich. The minority party traditionally votes for its leader, in this case House Democratic leader Richard Gephardt.
At least one Republican, Representative Christopher Shays of Connectict, says he will abstain from voting if the ethics issue remains unresolved at that time.
